newsitem.title: CHILE: Latin American stocks seen steady this week.
newsitem.headline: Latin American stocks seen steady this week.

text.p: Stocks on most of Latin America's main bolsas were expected to hold roughly flat this week, with some chance for light end-of-the-year rallies in Mexico and Chile, brokers said.
In the year's final weeks, most bourses had a flat, directionless feel and were heavily influenced by Wall Street and chances of a Federal Reserve rate rise, brokers said.

''We should see reduced volatility and scant volume, with everyone keeping a low profile and waiting to see what happens on Wall Street,'' said Argentine broker Miguel Daneri of Boston Securities, speaking about Buenos Aires shares in an opinion summing up sentiment in much of the region.
Argentine stocks were seen little changed this week provided the U.S. Federal Reserve leaves interest rates unchanged, dealers said.
They saw no significant local factors affecting the blue- chip Merval index, which ended last week down 4.2 percent at 600.43 points largely on Wall Street jitters.

Next door in Chile, high interest rates and tight competition in the electrical sector have depressed the blue- chip IPSA to its lowest level this year, 89.14 points on Friday, off 0.45 percent for the week.
But bargain-hunters could help up nudge up the market in the year's final weeks, possibly up to 95 points, brokers said.
Any hint from the Central Bank or the Finance Ministry of a a relaxing in interest rates in early 1997 would have an immediate bullish effect, they said.

A modest upturn could also be expected in Mexico, where stocks lost 3.83 percent last week to levels that could make them more attractive to foreign buyers who typically look for new investments at this time of year, analysts said.
Mexican shares have been trapped recently in the 3,250-to- 3,350 band and are essentially following the same pattern they have been in since August, said brokers.
In Brazil, the trend for this week was difficult to predict due to the high volatility surrounding Monday's options settlement, particularly at Telebras.

''Everything will depend on today,'' one dealer said. ''If most holders at the 76-real strike price exercise today, it will be good for the market and define the trend through the end of the year. If not, the market will go down.''
As in all bourses this week, Sao Paulo brokers were keeping a close eye on the prospect of a U.S. interest rate rise.
The Sao Paulo bourse's Bovespa index fell 2.8 percent last week to end Friday at 66,802 points.
With no data due for release, Venezuelan stocks were expected to wallow in lazy and trendless trade ahead of Christmas.
Only some unforeseen glitch in the expected sales of state- owned banks of Banco de Venezuela and Banco Consolidado on Friday might stir the markets.
On Friday, the leading index ended flat for the week as stocks recovered from a Monday selloff by foreign investors prompted by fears of a rise in U.S. interest rates.
